paperInfo.paperName: Grade 7 Physical Edu & Arts — Paper 2 (Structured Bank)

questions.questionText: State two personal hygiene practices that a learner should follow before and after Physical Education.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** Two essential personal hygiene practices a learner should follow before and after Physical Education are: **(1) Wearing clean, breathable sports attire (shorts, T-shirt, and proper tied sports shoes)** rather than tight school uniforms or bare slippery feet when required; and **(2) Washing hands, face, and sweaty body parts thoroughly with soap and clean water—and changing back into dry school clothes—immediately after exercise** (alongside trimming long fingernails short so teammates are not scratched during netball or football) [4 marks].

Regular sweating opens skin pores and mixes moisture with playground dust and bacteria; leaving damp, sweaty clothes against skin after PE causes fungal skin rashes (ringworm), body odour, colds when sitting in windy classrooms, and germ transfer when eating lunch with unwashed hands. Trimming nails and removing sharp rings or watches before lessons prevents accidental cuts during ball sports.

In ZIMSEC PE & Arts 7130/2, state distinct habits cleanly (*before* PE vs *after* PE) and always explain *why* hygiene protects both your health and classmates’ safety on the field.

questions.questionText: Explain two reasons why a learner should warm up before exercise and give one suitable warm-up activity.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** A learner should **warm up** before vigorous exercise for two vital physiological reasons: **(1) Warming up raises muscle and core body temperature gradually**, increasing muscle elasticity and joint lubrication (synovial fluid) so sudden sprints or kicks do not tear hamstrings or sprain ankles [1.5 marks]; and **(2) It gently accelerates heart rate and breathing**, routing oxygen-rich blood smoothly to working skeletal muscles before intense play begins [1.5 marks]. One suitable Grade 7 warm-up activity is **3–5 minutes of light jogging around the court followed by dynamic arm circles, gentle high-knee marches, and controlled calf/quadriceps stretches** [1 mark].

Notice how warm-ups prepare the nervous system too: practising light passing and gentle sideways shuffling sharpens reaction speed and coordination before competitive drills start. Skipping warm-up to launch straight into max-effort sprinting shocks cold, stiff muscle fibres and is a leading cause of school sports cramps and pulled muscles.

ZIMSEC markers specifically look for *preventing muscle/joint injuries* AND *gradually raising heart rate/blood flow* plus a named age-appropriate warm-up activity rather than vague statements like "to run fast."

questions.questionText: Name three health-related or skill-related fitness components and briefly describe one of them.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** Three recognised fitness components are **(1) Cardiovascular endurance (stamina)**, **(2) Muscular strength**, and **(3) Agility** (other valid components include speed, flexibility, balance, coordination, muscular endurance, and reaction time) [3 marks]. **Cardiovascular endurance** is the ability of the heart, lungs, and blood vessels to supply oxygen steadily to working muscles over sustained periods—such as running an 800 m race or playing a full netball match without tiring rapidly [2 marks].

Sports scientists group fitness into **health-related components** (cardiovascular endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility, body composition) that protect everyday wellbeing, and **skill-related components** (agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time, speed) that sharpen sporting performance. For example, high **flexibility** helps a gymnast bend safely without muscle tears, whereas rapid **agility** helps a football striker change direction cleanly around defenders.

When answering 7130/2 fitness questions, do NOT write simply "running fast"—use exact ZIMSEC terminology (**cardiovascular endurance, flexibility, agility, coordination, muscular strength**) and give a crisp definition plus matching sporting example.

questions.questionText: Explain why a learner needs a balanced diet when participating in regular physical activity.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** An active learner needs a **balanced diet** (containing carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre, and water in right proportions) because **vigorous sport burns heavy energy reserves and causes microscopic muscle wear that only proper daily nutrients can fuel and repair** [2 marks]. Specifically, **carbohydrates** (sadza, brown rice, sweet potatoes) provide steady glycogen energy to run and play; **proteins** (beans, eggs, fish/kapenta, milk) rebuild and strengthen exercised muscle fibres; **vitamins and minerals** (citrus fruits, green vegetables) boost immunity and calcium-strong bones; and **water** replaces sweat losses to stop dehydration and heatstroke [2 marks].

Without enough balanced nutrition—for instance skipping breakfast before athletics trials or eating only sugary sweets—athletes run out of stamina early, suffer dizziness or painful muscle cramps, heal slowly from minor bruises, and perform poorly both in class and on the pitch.

ZIMSEC examiners award top marks when you name specific **food nutrient groups** and state the exact biological job each performs for an active young athlete.

questions.questionText: State three common sports injuries and give one immediate safe response for each.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [6 marks]:** Three common school sports injuries and their immediate safe first-aid responses are: **(1) Ankle or wrist sprain (stretched/torn ligament)** — apply **R.I.C.E.** immediately (**Rest** the injured limb, apply a wrapped **Ice** pack for 15 minutes to control swelling, gentle **Compression** bandage, and **Elevate** above heart level) [2 marks]; **(2) Open skin graze or bleeding cut** — wear disposable protective gloves if available, gently clean dirt away with clean water/saline, press sterile gauze firmly until bleeding stops, and cover with a clean plaster [2 marks]; and **(3) Muscle cramp or heat exhaustion** — stop activity immediately, move the learner into cool shade, sip clean water/oral rehydration fluid slowly, and gently stretch the cramped muscle [2 marks].

Never pull or violently massage a suspected **fracture (broken bone)** or try to snap a dislocated joint back into place—instead immobilise the limb calmly in its current position, keep the casualty warm and still, and alert the teacher/first-aider or nearby clinic immediately.

In ZIMSEC PE Paper 2, pairing each named injury clearly with a safe **first-aid step**—and remembering hygiene (**gloves / clean water on open wounds**) plus **R.I.C.E. for sprains**—guarantees full marks.

questions.questionText: Describe the pathway of air from the nose or mouth to the lungs.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** During inhalation, fresh oxygen-rich air enters the body through the **nose (where tiny hairs and sticky mucus filter dust and warm the air)** or mouth, passes down the **pharynx (throat)** and **larynx (voice box)** into the rigid ringed **trachea (windpipe)** [2 marks]. The trachea splits into two **bronchi** entering the left and right **lungs**, which branch into finer **bronchioles** ending in millions of microscopic, moist air sacs called **alveoli**, where oxygen diffuses straight into surrounding blood capillaries [2 marks].

During Physical Education games, leg and arm muscles respire much faster to generate energy, prompting the diaphragm and ribcage muscles to pump air deeper and faster along this exact respiratory airway so working muscles receive ample oxygen without early breathlessness.

Examiners check strict anatomical sequence (**Nose/Mouth → Pharynx/Larynx → Trachea → Bronchi → Bronchioles → Lungs/Alveoli**). Mixing up the **trachea (windpipe)** with the **oesophagus (food pipe)** is a common mistake that loses marks immediately.

questions.questionText: Explain two functions of the circulatory system during exercise.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** During vigorous exercise, the **circulatory system** (heart, blood vessels, and blood) performs two crucial roles: **(1) Faster oxygen and glucose delivery** — the heart beats faster and pumps stronger strokes so arterial blood carries abundant oxygen (bound to red blood cells) and dissolved glucose quickly to contracting skeletal muscles for aerobic energy production [2 marks]; and **(2) Rapid waste and excess heat removal** — venous blood collects rising toxic **carbon dioxide (CO₂)** and lactic acid from active muscles back to the lungs/liver for removal while routing excess body heat out toward dilated skin capillaries so sweat evaporation cools the athlete down [2 marks].

Notice how this immediately explains why a learner’s **pulse rate and skin warmth** rise sharply during a 400 m race and gradually calm down during cool-down walking afterward: heart output scales automatically to match cellular demand and regulate body temperature.

In ZIMSEC 7130/2, avoid saying only *"it pumps blood"*; explain **both incoming fuel/oxygen transport AND outgoing CO₂/heat removal** clearly to score all 4 marks.

questions.questionText: Explain how muscles, bones and joints work together to produce movement.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** Human movement happens when **bones, joints, tendons, and antagonistic muscles** act together like biological levers [1 mark]. **Bones** form the rigid structural framework (such as the humerus in the upper arm and radius/ulna in the forearm) connected cleanly at movable **joints** (such as the hinge elbow or ball-and-socket shoulder cushioned by cartilage and synovial fluid) [2 marks]. **Skeletal muscles** attach across joints onto bones via tough inelastic **tendons**; because muscles can only pull by contracting (shortening) and cannot push, they work in **antagonistic pairs**—for instance, as the **biceps contracts** and pulls the forearm upward to bend the elbow, the **triceps relaxes**; to straighten the arm, the triceps contracts while the biceps relaxes [2 marks].

Whenever a child kicks a football or tosses a netball, coordinated nerve signals trigger one muscle group to tighten across a synovial joint while its partner relaxes smoothly, creating strong, accurate movement without grating bones together.

Key ZIMSEC terminology that locks in full marks includes **joints (hinge / ball-and-socket)**, **tendons** attaching muscle to bone, **ligaments** holding bones together across joints, and **contraction / relaxation of antagonistic muscle pairs**.

questions.questionText: Give four rules that should be followed when taking part in aquatic activities near a dam, river or swimming pool.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** Four vital **aquatic safety rules** around dams, rivers, or school swimming pools are: **(1) Never swim alone or without trained adult/teacher supervision**; **(2) Never dive head-first into murky, shallow, or unfamiliar dam/river water** where hidden rocks, tree stumps, or broken glass may cause fatal neck injuries; **(3) Obey pool hygiene and non-running rules—no pushing friends, running on slippery tiles, or swimming in fast-flooded streams or lightning storms**; and **(4) Keep rescue aids (lifebuoy rings, long poles, ropes) close by and wear certified lifejackets when boating, remembering to "Reach or Throw, Don’t Go"** if someone is drowning [4 marks].

Zimbabwean schools emphasise river and dam safety strongly because rural flash floods and unmarked deep farm-dam drop-offs alongside **bilharzia** freshwater snails in untreated stagnant rivers pose severe drowning and health hazards to curious children during summer heat.

State four distinct safety rules clearly in full sentences rather than writing one repeated idea (*"be careful"*). Including the drowning-rescue rule **reach/throw with a stick or rope rather than jumping blindly into deep water** impresses markers strongly.

questions.questionText: Describe how a learner can improve performance in a short sprint without breaking safety rules.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** A learner can boost short-sprint speed legally and safely by perfecting biomechanics: **(1) Warm up thoroughly and use a controlled crouch/standing start**, leaning slightly forward from the start line on *"On your marks… Set… Go!"* while reacting sharply without false-starting [1.5 marks]; **(2) Drive hard with bent arms pumping front-to-back (cheek-to-hip)**, lift knees high over the balls of the feet, keep shoulders relaxed, and run **strictly inside your assigned straight lane** looking straight ahead until **past the finish line** rather than slowing down early or twisting to check rivals [1.5 marks]; and **(3) Check the running track is clear of stones/holes, wear proper gripping trainers, and cool down by walking gently** [1 mark].

Notice how technical sprint rules protect fairness AND physical safety: staying strictly within marked track lanes stops high-speed collisions between runners, while slowing down gradually *after* crossing the tape prevents sharp knee jolts and hamstring pulls.

ZIMSEC athletics markers reward crisp action cues (**drive knees, pump bent arms front-to-back, run on balls of feet, stay in your lane past the finish line**).

questions.questionText: Explain how a safe baton exchange can be performed in a relay race.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** A fast, safe **relay baton exchange** follows three clear rules: **(1) Both the incoming and outgoing runners stay strictly inside their assigned lane and within the marked 20-metre takeover zone** [1.5 marks]; **(2) Use the blind/non-visual upsweep or downsweep pass while running**—the outgoing sprinter accelerates ahead inside the zone, reaches one steady open hand backward on the cue word (*"Hand!"* or *"Stick!"*) without turning their head blindly into other lanes, and grips the baton cleanly pushed into their palm [1.5 marks]; and **(3) The outgoing runner holds the baton firmly without throwing it**, while the passer runs straight ahead calmly inside their lane until teammates clear the track so nobody trips or collides [1 mark].

Alternating passing hands cleanly (e.g., Runner 1 right hand → Runner 2 left hand → Runner 3 right hand → Runner 4 left hand) prevents awkward body crossovers and allows the baton to travel straight down the inside or centre of the lane at top speed without dropping.

Always highlight **inside the 20 m takeover zone**, **not throwing the baton**, and **clear verbal signal without bumping adjacent lanes** to secure every athletics mark.

questions.questionText: State four basic skills used in football and explain one of them.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** Four foundational **football (soccer) skills** taught in Grade 7 PE are: **(1) Passing** (inside-of-foot push pass or instep lofted pass), **(2) Dribbling** (controlling the ball closely while running), **(3) Trapping / Receiving** (cushioning a moving pass cleanly), and **(4) Shooting / Heading / Tackling safely** [2 marks]. Taking **Dribbling** as an example: a player keeps the ball close to their feet using gentle taps with both the inside and outside of the foot, keeps their **head up frequently to scan teammates and opponents**, uses balanced arm movement to shield the ball safely, and avoids reckless lunges or high studs [3 marks].

Clean fundamental technique directly boosts fair play and lowers playground ankle injuries: players who trap with soft ankle "cushioning" retain control smoothly instead of swinging wild kicks at bouncing balls near opponents’ shins.

Make sure you **list all four distinct skills first**, then give a **detailed step-by-step biomechanical breakdown of one chosen skill** rather than leaving bullet labels unexplained.

questions.questionText: Explain the roles of any two netball positions.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** Two key **netball positions** and their court duties are: **(1) Centre (C)** — allowed everywhere on court *except* inside both shooting circles; acts as the tireless playmaker linking defence and attack, taking alternate centre passes from the centre circle, feeding accurate passes toward Goal Attack and Goal Shooter, and dropping back to mark the opposing Centre [2 marks]; and **(2) Goal Shooter (GS)** — restricted strictly inside the attacking goal third and attacking shooting circle; works closely with Goal Attack to create open space, catch high feeds safely without stepping (*footwork rule*), and shoot cleanly into the hoop while respecting the **0.9 m (3-foot) obstruction rule** [2 marks]. (Equally valid: **Goal Keeper (GK)** defending the defensive third/circle, **Wing Attack (WA)**, **Wing Defence (WD)**, **Goal Defence (GD)**, **Goal Attack (GA)**.)

Netball’s strict spatial zones require **teamwork and disciplined court spacing**: because no single player may run end-to-end across all thirds, every teammate must move sharply into open passing triangles without breaking contact or obstruction rules.

ZIMSEC markers always check whether you stated **each position’s exact allowed court zones** alongside their primary attacking/defending duties!

questions.questionText: Describe two correct techniques for controlling and moving with a basketball.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** Two correct **basketball ball-handling and movement techniques** are: **(1) Controlled Dribbling** — push the basketball downward gently toward the court using your **fingertips (pads of spread fingers)** rather than slapping with flat palms, keep knees bent in an athletic stance at waist height or lower, use your non-dribbling arm lightly to shield, and keep your **head/eyes up** to spot open teammates instead of staring at the ball [2 marks]; and **(2) Triple-Threat Catch & Chest/Bounce Pass (plus Legal Pivoting)** — land on balanced feet when stopping without travelling, protect the ball at chest/chin level, keep one pivot foot planted firmly if rotating, and step forward into crisp two-handed chest or bounce passes without charging recklessly into defenders [2 marks].

Practising correct fingertip dribbling and controlled jump-stops prevents frequent beginners’ turnovers (**double-dribble** and **travelling**) while avoiding collisions and bruised fingers on tarmac courts.

Emphasise **fingertip control, waist-height bounce, eyes up**, and **landing/pivoting without travelling** to match exact ZIMSEC 7130/2 criteria.

questions.questionText: Describe how a player can perform a controlled forearm pass.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** To perform a clean, controlled **forearm pass (dig)** in volleyball: **(1) Move early into position behind the dropping ball** with feet shoulder-width apart, one foot slightly ahead, knees deeply bent, and weight balanced forward on the balls of the feet [1.5 marks]; **(2) Lock your hands together safely** (place one palm inside the other and lay thumbs parallel alongside—never interlocking fingers tightly) and stretch both arms straight down away from your chest to create a **flat, firm forearm platform** just above the wrists [1.5 marks]; and **(3) Meet the ball smoothly on your flat forearms**, extending your legs and hips gently upward to direct a calm high arc toward the setter rather than swinging wild bent arms or calling *"Mine!"* too late and colliding with teammates [1 mark].

Notice that power during a forearm pass comes smoothly from **lifting with bent knees and legs**, NOT swinging elbows violently over head height—wild arm swings bounce the ball wildly backward out of court.

Never hit a volleyball dig with clenched separated fists or forearms bent upward; clearly mention **flat joined forearm platform, straight locked elbows, bent knees, and calling the ball loudly** for team safety.

questions.questionText: Explain two ways a fielding team can reduce the attacking team's scoring opportunities.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** In striking and fielding games (such as cricket, rounders, or softball), a fielding team can slash the batting team’s scoring chances in two key ways: **(1) Smart fielding placement and aggressive backing-up**—spreading fielders alertly across wide gaps and behind the wicketkeeper/bases so hit balls are intercepted rapidly before rolling past boundaries, while a second fielder backs up every hard throw to prevent costly overthrow runs [2 marks]; and **(2) Tight, accurate bowling/pitching combined with crisp, clean one-handed pick-up and accurate throwing** directly over the bowler’s or base’s gloves to catch or run out risky batters before they complete runs safely [2 marks].

Team safety on the fielding diamond matters just as much as sharp tactics: batters must never sling bats carelessly behind them after hitting, and fielders keep clear eyes on the ball while avoiding blocking base runners’ paths dangerously.

State both **tactical positioning/backing up** AND **accurate bowling/catching/clean throwing** to demonstrate real tactical game mastery.

questions.questionText: Describe three safety measures for floor gymnastics.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** Three essential **safety measures for floor gymnastics** are: **(1) Lay clean, thick, non-slip landing mats seamlessly** across bare concrete or hard halls with zero gaps where toes or ankles could catch [1.5 marks]; **(2) Warm up wrists, neck, shoulders, and spine gently beforehand, wear snug sports kit without dangling jewellery, hair clips, or loose shoes**, and match skills strictly to learners’ current readiness [1.5 marks]; and **(3) Tuck the chin firmly to the chest on all forward rolls** (so weight rolls smoothly onto upper shoulders/back rather than straining the neck!) and use **trained teacher spotting / controlled spacing** so gymnasts never collide mid-tumbling [1 mark].

Correct forward-roll alignment—placing flat palms shoulder-width apart, looking between legs, tucking the chin down cleanly, and lifting hips evenly—turns a potentially risky neck-loading tumble into a safe, graceful athletic skill.

ZIMSEC markers especially prize **proper mats**, **warm-up/clear space**, and **chin-tucking / spotting** as concrete school-gym safety answers.

questions.questionText: Explain how rhythm and space can be used to improve a group dance.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** Two choreographic elements that elevate a group dance dramatically are **rhythm** and **spatial awareness (space)**: **(1) Using rhythm**—dancers keep strict **synchronised timing** to drumbeats (*ngoma*), hand-claps, or melody cues, varying slow expressive gestures with sharp double-time footwork so the entire ensemble hits accents cleanly as one unified pulse [2 marks]; and **(2) Using space**—choreographers vary **levels** (low crouched harvest steps vs high leaps), **pathways** (circular, diagonal, and linear patterns across the stage), and **personal/group spacing** so every dancer remains visible to the audience without crowding or colliding with peers on stage [2 marks].

In traditional Zimbabwean dances such as *Mbakumba*, *Muchongoyo*, or *Isitshikitsha*, alternating tight unison formations with crisp diagonal cross-stage entries keeps audiences captivated while leaving safe clearing room for flying sticks, shields, or quick turns.

Pair clear definitions of **rhythm (steady beat & accented timing)** and **space (levels, directions, pathways, safe spacing)** directly with how they improve visual impact and learner safety.

questions.questionText: Describe three features of an effective mass-display formation.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** Three hallmarks of an effective **Mass Displays formation** (as showcased at school sports days and Zimbabwe national celebrations) are: **(1) Clean, crisp geometric alignment and uniform spacing**—rows, diagonals, circles, or emblem shapes stay geometrically balanced with equal arm-length intervals so patterns read sharply from grandstands [1.5 marks]; **(2) Synchronised timing, uniform posture, and clear visual contrast**—every performer executes flags, hoops, or calisthenic arm movements at the exact same drumbeat/whistle cue while contrasting bright costume or ribbon colours [1.5 marks]; and **(3) Smooth, safe transition pathways**—groups march or glide along rehearsed floor grid markers into the next shape without tripping, dropping props, or colliding [1 mark].

Mass Displays combine gymnastics, rhythmic dance, and visual graphic formations into disciplined teamwork: practicing spacing pegs or floor tape markers during afternoon rehearsals guarantees even large primary school casts look seamless and safe under bright stadium sun.

Focus on **geometric symmetry/spacing**, **synchronised movement cues**, and **smooth safe transitions** rather than just *"nice uniforms."*

questions.questionText: Define tempo, pitch and dynamics in music.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [6 marks]:** Three fundamental musical elements taught in Grade 7 PE & Arts are: **(1) Tempo** — the **speed or pace** of the musical beat (how fast or slow a song is performed, e.g., slow *adagio* mournful lament vs brisk *allegro* celebratory dance) [2 marks]; **(2) Pitch** — how **high or low** a musical note or singing voice sounds depending on vibration frequency (e.g., high soprano bird whistle vs deep bass marimba key) [2 marks]; and **(3) Dynamics** — the **volume (loudness or softness)** of music and gradual volume changes such as getting louder (*crescendo*) or softer (*diminuendo*) to add drama and emotional expression [2 marks].

Coordinating all three brings school choir performances alive cleanly: keeping steady **tempo** keeps singers aligned without rushing, matching exact **pitch** prevents harsh off-key clashes during harmony parts, and balancing **dynamics** (for instance soft verses building smoothly into strong joyful choruses) moves listeners emotionally while protecting young voices from shouting hoarsely.

Beware the #1 ZIMSEC music exam trap: mixing up **tempo** (*speed*: fast/slow) with **dynamics** (*volume*: loud/soft) or **pitch** (*tone frequency*: high/low)! Giving crisp distinct definitions plus musical examples secures all 6 marks.

questions.questionText: Explain how a performer can keep a steady beat when accompanying a song.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** A performer can keep a rock-steady **beat (pulse)** while accompanying a song by **(1) Internalising and counting a clear steady pulse silently or tapping a gentle toe/foot** right from a counted lead-in (*"1–2–3–4"*) before starting to play [1.5 marks]; **(2) Locking attention onto the lead percussionist or *ngoma/hosho* timekeeper** rather than speeding up excitedly on familiar choruses or dragging on difficult verses [1.5 marks]; and **(3) Maintaining relaxed ergonomic wrist/arm posture** and practising slowly at first with a rhythmic clap, drumbeat, or metronome before lifting performance speed safely [1 mark].

Ensemble musicians often "rush the tempo" when nervous—especially during lively clapping songs—leaving dancers breathless and vocals tangled. Breathing calmly together before the first beat and watching the conductor or lead drummer anchors the whole group tightly together.

State practical musician habits (**counting bars evenly, foot-tapping subtly, watching the lead drummer/conductor, and rehearsing steadily**) clearly to earn every mark.

questions.questionText: Explain how an actor can use voice and body movement to communicate a character.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** An actor communicates a distinct character convincingly using **voice** and **body movement**: **(1) Vocal expression**—varying **volume projection** (so the back row hears clearly without straining), **tone, pitch, pace, and meaningful pauses** (for example, quick clipped words for an anxious messenger vs slow deep warm speech for a wise village elder) [2 marks]; and **(2) Physical / body movement**—using deliberate **posture, facial expressions, hand gestures, and stage walking pace** suited to the character’s age, status, and emotion (such as stooped weary shoulders vs confident upright stride) while moving safely around props and staying angled toward the audience [2 marks].

When dialogue and physical body language agree—such as lowering your gaze nervously while speaking softly in a hesitant tone—audiences immediately understand a character’s inner feelings even before the plot unfolds further.

In ZIMSEC Drama Paper 2, divide your response clearly into **Vocal techniques** (tone, pitch, pace, projection) and **Physical/Movement techniques** (posture, gesture, facial expression, safe stage blocking).

questions.questionText: Give three guidelines for effective group improvisation.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** Three golden guidelines for lively, respectful **group drama improvisation** are: **(1) Listen actively and say "Yes, and…" to teammates’ ideas**—accept whatever scene setting or character offer another actor establishes instead of flatly saying "No" and stalling the story [1.5 marks]; **(2) Stay in character, share stage space fairly, and allow everyone turns to speak** rather than one loud learner hogging the scene or whispering private jokes [1.5 marks]; and **(3) Maintain clear safety boundaries and clear scene focus**—never use real physical hits/pushes during stage fights (fake slow-motion reactions safely with distance!) and work steadily toward resolving a clear conflict cleanly [1 mark].

Successful classroom improvisation builds quick creative thinking, empathy, and confident oral English or ChiShona fluency because learners invent genuine dialogue on the spot without rigid scripts.

Include both **collaborative storytelling rules ("Yes, and…" / listening)** and **physical stage safety (no real contact / clear focus)** for maximum credit.

questions.questionText: Name four elements of visual art and explain two of them.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** Four core **elements of visual art** are **Line**, **Colour**, **Shape / Form**, and **Texture** (alongside **Space** and **Tone/Value**) [2 marks]. Explaining two cleanly: **(1) Line** is a continuous moving mark stretching between two points (straight, curved, zigzag, or thick/thin), used by artists to define outlines, show movement, or divide picture space [1.5 marks]; and **(2) Texture** describes how an artwork’s surface actually feels to touch (tactile texture in carved wood, coiled clay pots, or woven reed baskets) or *looks* like it feels visually through careful shading [1.5 marks].

Understanding elements of design helps Grade 7 learners transition from random scribbles to thoughtful composition: crisp bold **lines** guide viewers’ eyes directly toward key figures, while contrasting smooth **textures** against rough hatched strokes brings traditional pottery or stone sculpture drawings vibrantly to life—remembering too to handle carving tools and brushes safely when working on tactile media.

Always list **four genuine visual art elements** cleanly before explaining **two** in depth; do NOT confuse *principles* (symmetry, balance, rhythm) with *elements* (line, colour, shape, form, texture, tone, space).

questions.questionText: Explain how primary colours can be combined to create secondary colours.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** In traditional subtractive paint mixing, the three **primary colours**—**Red, Yellow, and Blue**—cannot be created by mixing any other paints, yet combining them in pairs creates the three bright **secondary colours**: **(1) Red + Yellow = Orange**; **(2) Yellow + Blue = Green**; and **(3) Blue + Red = Purple (Violet)** [3 marks]. Practically in the school art room, dip a clean rinsed brush first into the **lighter colour (such as Yellow)** before stirring in tiny amounts of the darker colour (Red or Blue) gradually on a mixing palette, wiping spills immediately so tables stay safe and paint jars uncontaminated [1 mark].

Varying proportions produces rich natural shades—adding extra yellow to green yields fresh spring grass green, whereas adding a drop more blue shifts toward deep forest evergreen for painting Zimbabwean landscapes. Keeping brushes rinsed between mixes stops whole jars from turning muddy brown.

Writing exact colour equations (**Red + Yellow = Orange; Yellow + Blue = Green; Blue + Red = Purple**) plus clean safe art-room mixing habits guarantees full marks.

questions.questionText: Describe two ways repetition and symmetry can be used in a Zimbabwean-inspired design.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **Repetition** and **symmetry** feature prominently across traditional Zimbabwean crafts—such as **chevron and herringbone stone patterns at Great Zimbabwe, Shona clay pot (*hari*) incisions, and Ndebele geometric murals/beadwork** [1 mark]. **(1) Repetition** repeats a chosen motif (diamonds, zigzags, triangles, or dots) at regular intervals around a pot border or woven Tonga basket, creating pleasing visual rhythm and unity across the surface [1.5 marks]; and **(2) Symmetry** balances identical shapes, colours, and motifs evenly on opposite sides of a central mirror line (bilateral symmetry) or around a centre point (radial symmetry), giving wall paintings and carved wooden headrests calm harmony and structural beauty [1.5 marks].

Working steadily with rulers, safe pencils, and natural earth pigments (*ochre, white kaolin clay, charcoal*) teaches learners precision pattern-making while connecting mathematics geometry directly with Zimbabwe’s rich indigenous design heritage.

ZIMSEC markers look for clear **definitions of both repetition and symmetry** grounded in authentic **local cultural art forms (clay pots, chevron patterns, beadwork, baskets)** rather than vague European examples.

questions.questionText: Explain why learners should value and preserve Zimbabwean artistic and cultural heritage.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** Preserving and valuing **Zimbabwean artistic and cultural heritage**—from *mbira* music, stone carving, and pottery to traditional dances and folk tales—is vital because **(1) it strengthens cultural pride, identity, and respect across generations (*Unhu/Ubuntu*)** so young Zimbabweans know their true roots and moral values rather than copying foreign cultures blindly [2 marks]; and **(2) living traditional arts generate sustainable jobs and community tourism**, turning indigenous basketry, marimba building, and soapstone sculpture into respected livelihoods while sharing respectful appreciation among diverse ethnic groups safely at school [2 marks].

Notice how celebrating heritage in school arts clubs—such as learning safe pottery firing, repairing *hosho* rattles, or performing local folk songs—keeps timeless ecological and community wisdom alive while fostering mutual tolerance among all Zimbabwean communities.

Link heritage preservation concretely to **cultural identity/pride**, **intergenerational wisdom**, and **economic/tourism livelihood benefits** for top Paper 2 marks.

questions.questionText: Where appropriate, relate your answer to safe participation at school. Explain why learners should value and preserve Zimbabwean artistic and cultural heritage.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** Preserving and valuing **Zimbabwean artistic and cultural heritage**—from *mbira* music, stone carving, and pottery to traditional dances and folk tales—is vital because **(1) it strengthens cultural pride, identity, and respect across generations (*Unhu/Ubuntu*)** so young Zimbabweans know their true roots and moral values rather than copying foreign cultures blindly [2 marks]; and **(2) living traditional arts generate sustainable jobs and community tourism**, turning indigenous basketry, marimba building, and soapstone sculpture into respected livelihoods while sharing respectful appreciation among diverse ethnic groups safely at school [2 marks].

Notice how celebrating heritage in school arts clubs—such as learning safe pottery firing, repairing *hosho* rattles, or performing local folk songs—keeps timeless ecological and community wisdom alive while fostering mutual tolerance among all Zimbabwean communities.

Link heritage preservation concretely to **cultural identity/pride**, **intergenerational wisdom**, and **economic/tourism livelihood benefits** for top Paper 2 marks.

questions.questionText: State four factors to consider when preparing a venue for an arts performance.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** Four vital factors to check when preparing a **performance venue** (school hall or open courtyard) for an arts event are: **(1) Audience and performer safety** — ensuring flat unobstructed floor surfaces, taped-down power cables, clear marked emergency exits, and adequate ventilation/shade [1 mark]; **(2) Acoustics and sound setup** — positioning microphones, marimbas, or choirs so voices reach the back row clearly without echoing or feedback [1 mark]; **(3) Clear lighting and stage sightlines** — arranging benches or seating so every viewer sees performers cleanly without harsh sun glare or dark shadowed corners [1 mark]; and **(4) Neat staging, backstage waiting area, and waste bins** so props move smoothly between acts and the school compound stays litter-free afterward [1 mark].

Inspecting stage edges, electric sockets, and bench stability before guests arrive prevents twisted ankles, stage falls, or electrical hazards during busy inter-house cultural festivals.

Give **four distinct logistical categories** (Safety/Exits, Sound/Acoustics, Lighting/Seating Visibility, Stage Space/Backstage Cleanliness) rather than four variations of *"sweep the room."*

questions.questionText: Explain how a learner should care for art tools and materials after a practical activity.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** Responsible care of **art tools and materials** after a practical class protects both equipment longevity and learner safety: **(1) Wash paintbrushes immediately in clean water** (not hot water for glued bristles) pressing gently back into pointed tips and storing them **bristles-up** or flat so hairs do not bend permanently [1.5 marks]; **(2) Seal paint lids, clay bags, and glue bottles tightly** so materials do not dry out or spill onto floors, and wipe desks clean [1 mark]; and **(3) Safely count, wipe dry, and store sharp tools (scissors, craft knives, lino cutters, needles) inside locked boxes/caddies blades-down**, washing all clay or paint off hands thoroughly with soap afterward [1.5 marks].

Leaving stiff acrylic paint to dry inside brushes ruins expensive school art kits after one lesson, while loose scissors or spilled soapy water left on art-room floors cause cuts and slips during the next class.

Pair **cleaning/sealing brushes & paints** directly with **safe storage of sharp tools and hand hygiene** for full Paper 2 marks.

questions.questionText: State three ways a traditional musical performance can be prepared for a school cultural event.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** A school can prepare an authentic **traditional musical performance** for a cultural day through three structured steps: **(1) Selecting a suitable indigenous song/dance piece and matching traditional instruments** (such as *ngoma* drums, *hosho*, *mbira*, or *marimba*) rooted respectfully in community heritage [1.5 marks]; **(2) Holding regular scheduled rehearsals** where drummers, singers, and dancers refine rhythm alignment, clear vocal harmonies, entry/exit lines, and safe stage choreography [1.5 marks]; and **(3) Checking costumes, props, instrument tuning/safety, and venue sound space beforehand** so straps do not snap or drums crack during the show [1 mark].

Involving local community elders or music teachers early ensures lyrics, drum patterns, and traditional regalia are presented accurately and respectfully rather than distorted.

Organise your three points chronologically (**Selecting & researching piece → Rehearsing ensemble rhythm & staging → Checking costumes, tuned instruments & safe stage setup**).

questions.questionText: Give three questions a learner can ask when discussing a finished artwork.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [3 marks]:** When thoughtfully discussing or critiquing a classmate’s finished **artwork**, a learner can ask three constructive questions: **(1) Message & Inspiration:** *"What story, theme, or feeling did you want viewers to notice most in this artwork?"* [1 mark]; **(2) Elements & Technique:** *"Why did you choose those specific colours, lines, or textures/materials, and how did you create that effect?"* [1 mark]; and **(3) Craftsmanship & Growth:** *"What part of the piece works best, and is there anything you might adjust or develop further next time?"* [1 mark].

Constructive art critique teaches learners to look beyond *"It looks nice"* toward deliberate artistic choices—observing contrast, proportion, balance, and tidy finishing—while speaking encouragingly so peers feel proud to experiment and grow.

Ensure every question asks specifically about **meaning/theme, visual elements/technique, and constructive craftsmanship** rather than negative teasing.

questions.questionText: Explain three ways teamwork can improve a Physical Education or Arts group activity.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** Strong **teamwork** transforms Physical Education and Arts group work in three ways: **(1) Smooth coordination and higher performance quality**—passing patterns in football/netball and tight harmonies in choir/mass displays succeed only when members anticipate one another’s timing rather than playing selfishly [1.5 marks]; **(2) Safe load sharing and mutual support**—partners spot safely during gymnastics, carry heavy mats or marimbas together, and encourage shy or tired classmates to finish strongly [1.5 marks]; and **(3) Fair problem-solving and conflict resolution**—teammates listen respectfully when choosing choreography or defending strategies, turning diverse talents into one confident, unified school squad [1 mark].

Zimbabwean sport and cultural groups consistently out-perform isolated individual stars when teammates back each other up across defence, rehearsal setup, and post-match cleanup.

Link teamwork specifically to **coordinated game/art execution**, **physical safety/shared chores**, and **inclusive emotional encouragement**.

questions.questionText: State three ways learners can help keep a sports or performance environment safe and clean.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** Learners keep sports fields and arts performance areas safe and spotless through three consistent habits: **(1) Pre-activity hazard sweeps**—walking across pitches or stages beforehand to pick up broken glass, sharp stones, thorns, or loose cables before anyone runs or performs barefoot [1.5 marks]; **(2) Proper litter bins and equipment racks**—putting plastic water bottles, fruit peels, and snack wrappers straight into bins instead of fields, and returning balls, cones, drums, and props neatly to storage rooms after sessions [1.5 marks]; and **(3) Safe traffic and hygiene practices**—keeping spectators cleanly behind boundary lines away from active throwing/sprinting lanes and leaving toilets and changing areas dry and clean [1 mark].

Daily five-minute learner field sweeps dramatically cut cut-foot injuries, ankle twists from stray balls, and costly lost school equipment across every school term.

State **hazard inspection before play**, **litter/waste control**, and **tidy equipment storage + clear spectator boundaries** clearly for every mark.

questions.questionText: Suggest three simple ways a Grade 7 learner could responsibly use an Arts or sport skill to create value in the community.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** A Grade 7 learner can responsibly apply an **Arts or sport skill** to create positive value in their community in three practical ways: **(1) Coaching younger children or organising safe weekend village mini-leagues/games clubs** that keep peers physically fit and away from risky street hangouts or substance abuse [2 marks]; **(2) Crafting functional or decorative art sustainably from recycled or local materials** (such as beaded crafts, woven baskets, painted awareness posters on handwashing/anti-littering, or repaired school props) to beautify clinics/schools or raise small funds for stationery [1.5 marks]; and **(3) Performing community-education songs, skits, or traditional dances** at clinic days or clean-up campaigns to spread vital public-health and tree-conservation messages joyfully [1.5 marks].

Using sport and artistic creativity in community service builds early entrepreneurial confidence alongside **Unhu/Ubuntu** civic leadership—showing young learners that talent creates both joy and practical social good when shared responsibly.

Combine **healthy youth sport mentorship**, **sustainable art/craft posters or upcycling**, and **public-awareness creative performances** cleanly to cover both Arts and PE domains.
